The rain was coming down so hard that the last bus left in twenty minutes, and Rekha still had a box of laddoos to deliver. She ran the last stretch to the community hall, soaked, hair dripping onto the box.

Charu Ma'am, who led the Sunday meditation circle, had sat with her every week through the worst year of her life, never asking for anything. Rekha wanted to say thank you properly.

At the door she heard the announcement: everyone was being asked to give something for a new hall.

Rekha put in a little. Then she asked, "Ma'am, will the accounts be shown at the meeting?"

Charu Ma'am beamed. "Please ask that there too. I'd worry if no one did."

Rekha ran for the bus, smiling.

qa.q: What was Rekha carrying to give Charu Ma'am?
qa.a: Rekha was carrying a box of laddoos.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling about Charu Ma'am, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Deep thanks: she ran through the rain with laddoos for the teacher who had sat with her every week through the worst year of her life.

qa.q: What shows Rekha's thanks and clear thinking together?
qa.a: She gave a little to the new hall and still asked whether the accounts would be shown, so she supported the good while continuing to think. 🙂

qa.q: How does Charu Ma'am react to being questioned?
qa.a: Charu Ma'am is glad and says she would worry if no one asked, which shows a teacher who welcomes questions.

grounding: Rekha feels deep thanks for a teacher who helped her through a dark year, yet still asks a question about the money.

passage:
Dear Damini,

I haven't written in weeks because I didn't know how to say this. Last Sunday I went to bring the teacher a book and ended up in the private wing. A marble hall, cars I had never seen in the courtyard, and two staff members who quickly shut a door when I came near. The teacher has always told us that owning nothing is freedom.

I cried on the bus home. It felt like losing someone. Then I got angry and told myself I'd throw away everything I learned there, the morning silence, the telling of truth, all of it.

But last night I sat quietly anyway, and the stillness was still mine. So I'm keeping that. It's the person I'm still grieving.

Write back when you can.

Tanvir

qa.q: What did Tanvir go to bring the teacher?
qa.a: Tanvir went to bring the teacher a book.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel on the bus, and what did the anger make Tanvir want?
qa.a: It felt like losing someone, so Tanvir cried, then became angry and wanted to throw away everything learned there.

qa.q: What did Tanvir keep, and why is that wise?
qa.a: Tanvir kept the stillness and the telling of truth, separating the practice from the person, so grief over the teacher does not wipe out every value. 🤍

qa.q: How might Damini feel on reading this letter?
qa.a: Damini may feel concerned and want to comfort Tanvir, since the letter ends by asking for a reply after weeks of silence.

grounding: Tanvir discovers the teacher's luxury and secrets, grieves the image, keeps the truth learned and separates the practice from the person.

passage:
Counselling note, Alka, college counsellor.

Jasleen came in for the third time this month. The question is always the same: what would Guruji say? Before choosing an elective, before replying to a cousin's wedding invitation, even before picking a hostel room, Jasleen messaged the teacher first. Today Jasleen said, "If I choose without asking, I feel lost, like standing on a floor with no ground." Jasleen is not upset with the teacher, who seems kind.

I did not tell Jasleen to stop asking. I suggested two small choices to make alone this week: what to eat for lunch, and which seat to take in class. Jasleen agreed to jot down how each went and bring the note next Thursday.

I will also ask, gently, what a good guide would want Jasleen to grow into.

qa.q: How many times had Jasleen come to see the counsellor this month?
qa.a: Jasleen had come in for the third time this month.

qa.q: How does Jasleen feel when choosing without asking the teacher?
qa.a: Jasleen feels lost, describing it as standing on a floor with no ground.

qa.q: What small step did Alka suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Alka suggested two small choices alone, lunch and a class seat, then a note on how each went, so Jasleen can see that Jasleen can decide. 🙂

qa.q: What would change if the teacher encouraged Jasleen to build judgement?
qa.a: The guidance would grow Jasleen's own judgement instead of dependence, and Jasleen might feel less lost over time.

grounding: Jasleen asks the teacher before every decision and feels lost without asking, and the counsellor sets small solo choices to build judgement.

passage:
Omkar spotted Tushar at the college canteen counter, thinner, in plain white clothes, collecting papers for the ashram. Three months ago Tushar had stopped answering his parents' calls. Omkar's chest tightened.

"Come sit. Tea?"

Tushar hesitated, then sat. "I've only got ten minutes. The group is waiting."

Omkar wanted to say the teacher was using him. Instead he swallowed it. "What's a normal day like there?"

Tushar lit up, talking about songs at dawn and cooking for two hundred people.

"Sounds like real work," Omkar said. "You don't have to answer, but people ask about you. My door is open, any time, even midnight."

Tushar looked at his tea. "Okay," he said quietly.

qa.q: Where did Omkar spot Tushar?
qa.a: Omkar spotted Tushar at the college canteen counter.

qa.q: What was Omkar worried about, and why did Omkar swallow the urge to say the teacher was using Tushar?
qa.a: Omkar was worried about Tushar cutting off his parents, and held back because attacking the teacher might make Tushar defensive and push him further in.

qa.q: What would you advise Omkar to do next?
qa.a: Stay warm, keep asking curious questions, keep the door open for Tushar to visit or call, and avoid ultimatums or attacks on the teacher.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel when asked about a normal day?
qa.a: Tushar lit up talking about songs at dawn and cooking, so a curious question probably felt welcoming rather than judging, which made it easier to say okay to the open door.

grounding: Omkar worries about a friend who cut off his family for the ashram and responds with warmth and curiosity, not ultimatums or attacks.

passage:
Dear Vasudha,

Sorry I've been quiet. I've been going to a new circle that meets near college, and I wanted to tell you before you hear it from someone else.

Honestly, this first week has been the warmest I've felt since last year. Someone saved me a seat. Someone remembered my name and how I take my tea. They cook and eat together and keep telling me, "You belong here." After such a lonely year, I cried a little in the washroom from relief.

One small thing: a member said it might be better to see my old friends less "until you settle in". I said I'd think about it. I'm going to keep our Sunday calls. I like the kindness. I just want to keep watching what it asks of me.

Love,
Pooja

qa.q: What did someone remember about Pooja?
qa.a: Someone remembered Pooja's name and how Pooja takes tea.

qa.q: Why did Pooja cry in the washroom?
qa.a: It was relief: after such a lonely year, the warmth and the words "You belong here" meant a great deal.

qa.q: How is Pooja handling the suggestion to see old friends less?
qa.a: Pooja neither rejects the kindness nor accepts the suggestion, keeping the Sunday calls while watching what the group asks.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel reading Pooja's letter?
qa.a: Vasudha may be glad that Pooja feels warm again and a little concerned about seeing old friends less, so the promise to keep the Sunday calls would reassure.

grounding: Group members shower Pooja with attention and belonging after a lonely year, and Pooja enjoys it while noticing a request to see old friends less.

passage:
In the kasba, Karthik had been going to the meditation house behind the grain market for two months. This week the leader made three requests in one breath: a donation "for your growth", the phone handed over "to quiet the mind", and no more visits to old friends who "drag you down".

Karthik walked to Sabina's tea stall afterwards with the phone still in a pocket, and sat without ordering.

"You look like someone swallowed your tongue," Sabina said.

Karthik repeated the three requests slowly. Said aloud, they sounded different.

Sabina put down the kettle. "Money, phone, friends. That's how you control someone, not how you grow them. Keep your phone. Keep your own money. Keep coming here. And call your uncle in the city before you decide anything."

For the first time all week, Karthik took the phone out.

qa.q: Where did Karthik walk after the leader's requests?
qa.a: Karthik walked to Sabina's tea stall.

qa.q: Why did Karthik sit at the stall without ordering?
qa.a: Karthik was unsettled by the three requests and needed someone outside the meditation house, which the silence and slow repeating of the requests show.

qa.q: What would you advise Karthik about the phone, money and friends?
qa.a: Keep the phone and own money, keep seeing old friends, keep a way to leave, and call the uncle in the city or another outsider before deciding.

qa.q: How does Sabina see the leader's three requests?
qa.a: Sabina sees money, phone and friends together as a way to control someone, not help them grow.

grounding: Karthik is asked to donate, surrender the phone and drop old friends, and an outsider names these as control signals.

passage:
I'm Lalit, Chaitanya's roommate, and I'm writing down what I saw because I'm not sure what to make of it.

Last Saturday Chaitanya's parents asked about the group over dinner. Chaitanya defended it for twenty minutes, sitting straight, repeating that they're the only people who really listen. It sounded rehearsed, though maybe that's simply how belief sounds.

Later, while we folded clothes, Chaitanya went quiet and asked me, "Do you think you can ask the leader anything?" Then quickly: "Never mind, ignore that." Chaitanya opened the group chat, stared at it, and put the phone down without typing.

The group's old photos are still pinned above the desk. I don't know what is going on inside. I only know the question got swallowed.

qa.q: For how long did Chaitanya defend the group at dinner?
qa.a: Chaitanya defended the group for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What might Chaitanya be feeling when asking whether you can ask the leader anything?
qa.a: Private doubt mixed with the pull to belong; the question, the quick "Never mind" and the unsent message suggest Chaitanya wanted to ask but felt it might not be allowed, though Lalit cannot be sure.

qa.q: How could Lalit support Chaitanya?
qa.a: Lalit could stay warm, invite Chaitanya to say more without pressure, and gently wonder aloud which questions feel off limits.

qa.q: How does Lalit see Chaitanya's defence at dinner?
qa.a: Lalit found it rehearsed but admits it may simply be how belief sounds, so Lalit holds the observation loosely.

grounding: Chaitanya defends the group while private doubts grow, and an observer notices a question that goes unasked.

passage:
I'm Francis, and I live next door to Samir's family, so I saw this from our balcony.

Samir's parents stood at the gate for an hour. The mother kept saying, "Just come home for dinner. One dinner." The father held a tiffin. Samir stayed at the gate with arms crossed, saying, "You don't understand. You're against us. The group is my real family." The mother's voice shook. Samir turned away.

Later that night, Samir's younger sister came out, and Samir sat with her on the steps for a while, laughing quietly. Samir took the tiffin from her, ate half of it, and went back inside without a word.

I can't say what Samir thinks. But it looked to me like one thread stayed.

qa.q: How long did Samir's parents stand at the gate?
qa.a: They stood at the gate for an hour.

qa.q: What does Samir seem to think of the family at the gate, and what hints at something softer?
qa.a: At the gate Samir sees them as against the group and says they don't understand, but sitting with the sister and eating half the tiffin hints at lingering warmth, though Francis cannot be sure.

qa.q: What would you advise Samir?
qa.a: Listen for the love inside the parents' fear, such as their plea for one dinner, and keep at least one connection alive while disagreeing.

qa.q: How might Samir's mother feel at the gate?
qa.a: The mother is likely frightened and pleading; her shaking voice and repeated request for one dinner show love more than a wish to fight.

grounding: Samir's family begs Samir to leave the group and Samir sees them as enemies, yet one thread of connection stays, as an observer sees.

passage:
Thursday, late

Today I finally said it aloud to Parveen, the college counsellor: the group's promises don't match what they do. They said everyone is equal, but the leaders ate separately and never answered when we asked where the donations went. They said "we are family", but when a member wanted to go home for a wedding, they were called weak.

For three years I gave them my weekends, my savings, my friends. I feel so foolish. I keep counting those years as if they were stolen.

Parveen said that walking away took courage, not foolishness, and asked if I'd come every week. I said yes. I also told my sister. She cried and hugged me.

Slowly. That's the plan. I'm allowed to grieve.

Imran

qa.q: To whom did Imran say it aloud today?
qa.a: Imran said it aloud to Parveen, the college counsellor.

qa.q: Why does Imran feel foolish?
qa.a: For three years Imran gave the group weekends, savings and friends, and now keeps counting those years as if they were stolen.

qa.q: What supports are helping Imran, and what else could help?
qa.a: Talking to Parveen, coming every week and telling the sister help, and allowing grief while rebuilding slowly adds to that.

qa.q: How might Imran's sister be seeing this change?
qa.a: Imran's sister cried and hugged Imran, which suggests relief and love, and perhaps that she had been worried.

grounding: Imran sees the group's promises did not match its actions, feels foolish and grieves, and starts rebuilding with support.

passage:
On the community centre notice board, a small card read: "Support hour for people who've left groups, Thursday 5 pm." Nandini almost walked past it. She sat in the back row, twisting her scarf.

Sunaina, the volunteer at the front, told her story briefly. "I was scared to leave too. I thought everything bad would happen. Two years on, my days are quiet, and I sleep."

Nandini felt her shoulders drop. "You were scared like this?"

"Exactly like this. But don't take my word as a new rule. You decide. If you like, this week we just talk to your cousin first, nothing more."

Nandini nodded. For the first time in months she didn't feel like the only person on earth with these thoughts.

qa.q: When is the support hour?
qa.a: The support hour is on Thursday at 5 pm.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel after hearing Sunaina's story, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Less alone and calmer: her shoulders dropped and she no longer felt like the only person with these thoughts.

qa.q: Why is one step this week, talking to the cousin, a good choice?
qa.a: It is one safe step at a time and leaves the decision with Nandini, instead of replacing one authority with another.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel telling her story?
qa.a: Sunaina likely feels empathy and wants to help without pushing, shown by warning Nandini not to take the story as a new rule.

grounding: An ex-member shares that she felt the same fears and now finds peace, so Nandini feels less alone and takes one safe step.
